Why Rising Rates Could Break the Bull Market Before AI Spending Can Save It Chevron (NYSE:CVX) reported third-quarter 2026 earnings of $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, as record U.S. refinery crude throughput and nearly 4 million barrels per day of production helped support operating performance. Adjusted earnings totaled $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share, while cash flow from operations excluding working capital was $16.6 billion. Chairman and CEO Mike Wirth said the company delivered its fifth consecutive quarter of U.S. upstream production above 2 million barrels per day. Chevron also recorded strong results across its refining network, natural-gas portfolio and major international assets, while advancing growth options in Venezuela, Angola, Iraq and other regions. → Heavy Metal: Why Nucor Could Be an Overlooked AI Infrastructure Winner How a Hurricane Could Help Some Refineries—and Hurt Others CFO Eimear Bonner said adjusted earnings declined $1.6 billion from the prior quarter. Upstream earnings were lower because of reduced realizations, lower liftings and unfavorable timing effects, partly offset by lower depreciation, depletion and amortization expense and tax effects. Downstream earnings increased as higher refining margins and volumes outweighed unfavorable timing effects. Chevron generated $14.2 billion of adjusted free cash flow during the quarter. Bonner said fourth-quarter spending is expected to rise from third-quarter levels, though Chevron still expects to finish 2026 at the low end of its annual capital-spending guidance. Management said it does not plan to change its capital-allocation framework despite its strengthened balance sheet. Bonner reiterated Chevron's priorities of growing its dividend, investing efficiently, maintaining a strong balance sheet and repurchasing shares through the cycle. The company maintained its buyback range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. → Johnson Controls Beats the Heat in AI Data Centers "We're on track with our 2030 plan that we guided in the investor day," Bonner said, adding that Chevron expects to provide more detail on its 2027 capital program following a December board meeting. Chevron outlined plans to increase gross production from its three Venezuelan joint ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, from about 300,000 barrels per day expected by year-end. Wirth said the program would rely on primary recovery, be self-funding and could extend further into the 2030s. The company expects total costs in Venezuela to be below $20 per barrel, including capital and operating costs. Bonner said Chevron does not anticipate major new infrastructure spending to support the production increase, describing the program as a "factory-like operation" that could become more efficient over time. Wirth said revised fiscal terms have made Venezuela more competitive in Chevron's portfolio and immediately accretive to free cash flow. Chevron markets all crude produced from the three ventures, with most volumes going to U.S. refineries including Pascagoula and El Segundo. Addressing risk in the country, Wirth cited contract provisions including stability clauses and international arbitration. He also said Chevron's control of crude marketing and revenue flows, along with its intention to fund development through venture-generated cash flow, differentiates the current arrangement from prior structures. Elsewhere, Chevron said it continues negotiations on an extension of its Tengizchevroil, or TCO, concession in Kazakhstan. Wirth said discussions have progressed over more than a year, with technical, commercial and legal teams narrowing the issues to "fundamental core issues." Chevron increased capacity at TCO's third-generation plant by 20%, lifting total processing capacity to slightly above 1 million barrels per day. title: Chevron Profit Nearly Triples as Refining Hits Record - TradingView
content: Chevron CVX delivered a blowout third quarter, with profit nearly tripling as stronger crude realizations and record refinery throughput lifted earnings across both its upstream and downstream businesses. The oil major reported $9.9 billion in net income, or $5.06 per share, up from $3.5 billion, or $1.82 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EPS came in at $5.28, comfortably ahead of Wall Street expectations, while revenue surged 36.3% year over year to $67.8 billion. Chevron shares rose about 1.6% in premarket trading Friday. Chevron said refinery crude throughput hit a record 1.09 million barrels per day, with crude-unit capacity utilization approaching 98%. That helped U.S. downstream earnings jump to $3.58 billion from just $638 million a year earlier, as higher refined-product margins combined with unusually strong refinery utilization. International downstream earnings also climbed sharply to $1.34 billion from $499 million, although refined-product sales fell 9% because of Middle East supply disruptions. Chevron's average U.S. crude oil and NGL sales price rose 30% to $62.72 per barrel, while international realizations climbed 36% to $86.09 per barrel. U.S. upstream earnings rose to $3.29 billion from $1.28 billion, while international upstream earnings improved to $2.4 billion from $2.02 billion. Worldwide output fell 2.6% to 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, reflecting lower entitlements tied to higher prices and disruption from the Middle East conflict. Still, Chevron posted record production at operated assets in Australia, higher output in the U.S. Gulf, and one month of Venezuelan production. Operating cash flow surged to $16 billion from $9.4 billion, helped by higher earnings and larger distributions from Tengizchevroil. Chevron also cut total debt by another $3.5 billion, while net debt declined by $7.8 billion during the quarter. The company declared a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. I think the most important part of Chevron's quarter is that the earnings strength was broad-based rather than dependent on one business line. Higher oil prices helped upstream profits, but refining did just as much heavy lifting. Record throughput and near-full refinery utilization turned Chevron's downstream business into a major earnings engine, with U.S. downstream profit increasing more than fivefold from a year earlier. That matters because it gives Chevron another source of earnings leverage when refining margins are favorable. With $16 billion in operating cash flow and net debt down $7.8 billion in a single quarter, Chevron has more balance-sheet flexibility for dividends, buybacks and future investment. For investors, the key things to watch are refining margins, oil realizations, Middle East disruptions, production growth and whether record refinery utilization can be sustained. title: Chevron (NYSE:CVX) delivers strong Q3 2026 numbers - The Globe and Mail
content: Integrated energy company Chevron (NYSE:CVX) reported revenue ahead of Wall Street’s expectations in Q3 2026, with revenue rising 36.3% year on year to $67.8 billion. Its non-GAAP profit of $5.28 per share was 8.5% above analysts’ consensus estimates. For more on Chevron, read our free full research report. “We’re reinvesting to bring more energy to a supply-constrained market,” Wirth continued. In Venezuela, Chevron’s joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of generating low-cost, high-return and long-duration production growth. In the United States, the company signed agreements to reduce Bakken midstream costs by approximately 50 percent, strengthening the asset’s competitiveness. “Building on our performance this quarter, we're focused on delivering the reliable energy the world needs today, while positioning Chevron for the future,” Wirth concluded. A company’s long-term performance can give signals about its business quality. Even a bad business, especially in a cyclical industry, can perform well for a year or so, but a top-tier one should exhibit resilience through cycles. Over the last five years, Chevron grew its revenue at a decent 10.8% compounded annual growth rate. Its growth was slightly above the average energy upstream and integrated energy company and shows its offerings resonate with customers. Even a long stretch in energy can be shaped by a single commodity cycle, so extending the view to ten years adds another perspective and reveals which companies are built to grow regardless of the pricing regime. Chevron’s annualized revenue growth of 7.6% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results were still good. While looking at revenue is important, it can also introduce noise around commodity prices and M&A. Analyzing production, on the other hand, highlights what is happening inside the asset base and whether the economic footprint of a company is expanding. Over the last two years, Chevron’s oil production averaged 14.1% year-on-year growth while its natural gas production averaged 14.4% year-on-year growth. This quarter, Chevron reported strong year-on-year revenue growth of 36.3%, and its $67.8 billion of revenue exceeded Wall Street’s consensus estimates by 11.1%. Chevron also reported modest year-on-year oil production growth of 0.1%. Adjusted EBITDA margin strips out accounting distortions tied to depletion and historical drilling spend, providing a clearer view of the cash-generating power of the underlying asset base before financing and reinvestment decisions. Chevron was profitable over the last five years but held back by its large cost base. Its average EBITDA margin of 25.3% was weak for an upstream and integrated energy business. On the positive side, Chevron’s EBITDA margin rose by 1.2 percentage points over the last year, as its revenue growth gave it operating leverage. This quarter, Chevron generated an EBITDA margin of 29.3%, up 5.9 percentage points year on year. The increase was a positive sign of greater efficiency. Adjusted EBITDA fell short of Wall Street’s consensus estimates. Adjusted EBITDA shows how profitable a company’s existing “rock” is before financing and reinvestment, while free cash flow shows how much value remains after paying to replace those wells. Because production declines over time, strong EBITDA can coexist with weak FCF if drilling is expensive or declines are steep. FCF therefore captures both operating efficiency and the cost of sustaining production. Chevron has shown strong cash profitability, giving it the option to reinvest or return capital to investors. The company’s free cash flow margin averaged 11.6% over the last five years, better than the broader energy upstream and integrated energy sector. The level of free cash flow is important, but its durability across cycles is just as critical. Consistent margins are far more valuable than volatile swings driven by commodity prices. Chevron’s ratio of quarterly free cash flow volatility to WTI crude price volatility over the past five years was 4.9 (lower is better), indicating strong insulation from commodity swings. This stability supports capital access in downturns and positions Chevron to act as a consolidator when weaker peers are forced to retrench. Why use free cash flow to assess stability against commodity prices rather than compare Chevron’s revenue or EBITDA to WTI? What ultimately matters is not how much revenue or profit a company earns when prices are high but how much cash it can generate when prices are low. Free cash flow is the superior metric because it captures hedging effectiveness, growth and maintenance capex and management behavior during good times and bad. Chevron’s free cash flow totaled $12 billion in Q3, equivalent to a 17.7% margin. This was a positive result, as its margin was 7.8 percentage points higher than in the same quarter last year. Its cash profitability was also above its five-year level. Chevron delivered a solid quarter, with revenue well ahead of analysts’ consensus estimates and EPS also topping Wall Street’s estimates. Shares edged higher 1.6% to $235.02 immediately after the release. Chevron had a solid quarter, but is the stock a buy? The latest quarter is only one piece of the longer-term business quality puzzle. Quality, when combined with valuation, can help determine if the stock is a buy. CVX reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings on Friday as disruptions to global fuel supplies lifted refining margins, helping the oil major offset weaker contributions from its oil and gas production business. The company reported net income of $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, compared with $3.5 billion, or $1.82 per share, in the same period last year. Adjusted earnings, excluding special items and foreign currency effects, came in at $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share, beating the average analyst estimate of $4.89, according to LSEG data. Revenue reached approximately $67.8 billion, beating estimates comfortably. Chevron’s downstream division, which includes refining and fuel sales, generated $4.9 billion in earnings, more than four times the $1.1 billion recorded a year earlier and slightly higher than the previous quarter. The improvement came as attacks on refining facilities in Russia and the Middle East disrupted fuel production, tightening supplies of diesel and other refined products and pushing margins higher. Chevron’s US refineries processed a record more than 1 million barrels of crude per day during the quarter, with the facilities running at 98% capacity. Production yields of diesel and jet fuel also increased by more than 10%, reflecting strong demand for refined products. The upstream business, which covers oil and gas exploration and production, generated $5.7 billion in earnings. Although higher than the $3.3 billion reported a year earlier, the figure declined 30% from the second quarter as crude prices eased. Worldwide production averaged 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, down 2% from the previous quarter. The company also recorded its first month of equity-accounted production from Venezuela under improved fiscal terms, with total production costs below $20 per barrel. However, production in the third quarter of 2026 was lower than a year ago primarily due to lower entitlements from higher prices and impacts from the Middle East conflict Cash flow from operations reached $16 billion, while adjusted free cash flow climbed to $14.2 billion, twice the level recorded a year earlier. Chevron distributed $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion worth of shares during the quarter. Net debt declined to $20.7 billion from $34.5 billion at the end of 2025. title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars - CNBC
content:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices. Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday. The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street’s expectations. “Refining capacity is very tight today,” Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. “Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand.” U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September. Chevron’s net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street’s expectations of $4.89. “The system is under stress,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. “We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile.” Here’s what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon “were making too much money based on a shortage.” The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Profits from Chevron’s refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. Chevron’s U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said. Exxon’s refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business’ earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Exxon’s Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced “record volumes of diesel” in the quarter, Woods said. Chevron’s oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year. Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.                         Patricia Miller Chevron beat third-quarter profit estimates as record U.S. refinery runs lifted fuel earnings, while its oil and gas output dipped on Middle East disruptions. Chevron's third quarter shows how much refining now drives its profit, as war-related supply disruptions widened fuel margins and its U.S. plants ran at record rates. That offset a dip in international output. Management is using the cash to cut debt and expand in Venezuela, though price swings, conflict and fuel politics remain risks. Chevron Corporation (NYSE: CVX) on Friday reported third-quarter profit of $9.9 billion, nearly triple the year-earlier figure and ahead of analyst forecasts, as its U.S. refineries processed a record volume of crude and fuel margins widened. Adjusted earnings were $5.28 per share, compared with the $4.89 analysts had expected, according to LSEG. The result came as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine disrupted global energy supply. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on refineries in Saudi Arabia and Russia took fuel-making capacity offline, lifting margins for U.S. refiners running near full rates. Chevron's downstream earnings were the highest in at least six years. Revenue and other income totaled $67.8 billion, above the $61.6 billion analysts had forecast. Chevron shares rose about 2% in premarket trading on Friday. "We're reinvesting to bring more energy to a supply-constrained market," Mike Wirth, Chevron's chairman and chief executive officer, said in the earnings release. The company said U.S. upstream output topped 2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Downstream earnings rose to $4.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. The U.S. business accounted for $3.6 billion of that, up from $638 million, which the company attributed to higher margins on refined product sales. U.S. refinery crude throughput, the volume of oil the plants process, reached a record 1.09 million barrels per day, with crude unit utilization near 98%. Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner said in an interview that Chevron could grow capacity at its Pascagoula refinery in Mississippi by 7% by the end of the decade. Houston-based Chevron produces crude oil and natural gas and makes transportation fuels, lubricants and petrochemicals. It reports results across upstream production and downstream refining and marketing. Upstream earnings rose to $5.7 billion from $3.3 billion, helped by higher crude prices. Brent averaged $97 a barrel in the quarter, compared with $69 a year earlier. Total production fell to 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent per day from 4.09 million. The decline came from international operations, where output fell by 109,000 barrels per day. The company cited lower entitlements, meaning the smaller share of output it receives under some contracts when prices rise, and the Middle East conflict. Record output in Australia and higher Gulf of America production partly offset the drop. Profit was below the second quarter's $12.1 billion, as Brent eased from an average of $104 a barrel. Timing effects, accounting mismatches tied to derivatives and inventory values, reduced earnings by $1.58 billion in the quarter. Same news, different lens. Cash flow from operations rose to $16 billion from $9.4 billion a year earlier. Chevron reduced total debt by $3.5 billion during the quarter, while net debt fell by $7.8 billion to $20.7 billion. That compares with $34.5 billion at the end of 2025. "We think in decades, not quarters," Bonner said, describing a strong balance sheet as necessary through both high and low oil prices. Chevron bought back $2.5 billion of shares in the quarter and declared a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share, payable Dec. 10. The company said it secured improved commercial terms and more acreage in Venezuela, where its joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over the next five years. Chevron said the deal gives it the potential to more than double production there over that period. Chevron also signed agreements it said would cut Bakken midstream costs, the cost of moving and processing oil and gas, by about 50%. It reported an offshore discovery in Angola's Lower Congo Basin and signed an exploration agreement with Libya's National Oil Corporation. Bonner said Brent ranged from as low as $68 to as high as $132 a barrel during the quarter. Fuel prices have also become a political issue ahead of next Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, after President Donald Trump considered a diesel export ban in September before saying in early October he would not impose one. Wirth said Chevron is focused on supplying reliable energy now while positioning the company for the future, with the Venezuela and Bakken moves part of that plan. Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX, XETRA:CHV) reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share, beating analysts’ expectations as higher refining margins and stronger oil realizations helped drive a sharp increase in revenue. Higher oil price realizations and stronger refining margins drove earnings growth, helping the US oil major’s adjusted earnings per share beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.78 by 10.46%. Revenue for the three months ended September reached $67.8 billion, up 36.4% from $49.7 billion a year earlier and 12.09% above the Zacks consensus forecast. Reported earnings were $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per diluted share, compared with $3.5 billion, or $1.82 per share, in the same period last year. Adjusted earnings were $10.4 billion, compared with $3.6 billion a year earlier, reflecting stronger operating performance despite unfavorable foreign currency and timing effects. The upstream business generated earnings of $5.7 billion, compared with $3.3 billion a year earlier, while downstream earnings more than quadrupled to $4.9 billion from $1.1 billion. Higher margins on refined product sales supported the improvement, with US refineries achieving record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day and crude utilization approaching 98%. Chevron produced 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, slightly below 4.09 million a year earlier, as lower production entitlements and Middle East conflict-related impacts offset gains in Australia and the Gulf of America. Cash flow from operations reached $16 billion, compared with $9.4 billion a year earlier, while free cash flow increased to $12 billion from $4.9 billion. The company returned $6 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter and declared a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share, payable on December 10. Chief executive Mike Wirth said strong operational performance and disciplined execution had supported the results, while the company continued investing to expand energy supply. title: Chevron vs. Occidental Petroleum: Big Oil Sees Revenue Surge as Prices Leap in 2026 - The Motley Fool
content: Chevron's latest quarter surged to $67.2 billion while Occidental rebounded to $8.3 billion, marking a sharp reversal from their prior downtrend. Chevron Corp. (CVX +1.75%) primarily generates revenue by exploring for, developing, producing, and refining crude oil and natural gas globally, while simultaneously managing a multifaceted operational network that manufactures and distributes bulk petrochemicals, liquid fuels, and specialized industrial lubricants to a broad international customer base. It recently signed formal international agreements intended to update multiple joint venture operating provisions in Venezuela and independently confirmed a new oil and gas condensate discovery at an active offshore exploration well located in Angola. Occidental Petroleum Corp. (OXY +1.57%) primarily earns revenue by acquiring, exploring, and developing conventional oil and natural gas properties across the globe, alongside operating a distinct, specialized midstream marketing segment that purchases, processes, stores, and transports gathered carbon dioxide and power resources for various commercial applications. It recently appointed a new general counsel to manage legal affairs and experienced ongoing production suspensions at a natural gas field in the United Arab Emirates. Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item, which tracks incoming money and helps investors evaluate overall baseline business scale. For most stocks, compare revenue year over year by quarter. In normal times, that holds true for energy stocks as well--typically revenue rises in summertime as demand peaks because people, especially Americans, are driving more on holidays. title: AI Power Stocks Fell 7% to 13% in a Week While Exxon and Chevron Just Hit Record Highs. Here's Which Side I'd Rather Own. - The Motley Fool
content: Stocks like Oklo are high-risk, and the opportunity may not pan out, but Exxon and Chevron are built to survive hard times. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the hot topic on Wall Street and Main Street right now. But for those old enough to remember, the environment may be starting to feel like the dot-com bubble, which burst at the turn of the century. Companies like Oklo (OKLO -5.82%), NuScale Power (SMR -5.07%), and even Constellation Energy (CEG -0.83%) all fell around 7% from their highs over the last five days, as of this writing. Bloom Energy (BE -8.61%) is down 13% from its high in that shockingly short period. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil (XOM +2.16%) and Chevron (CVX +1.75%) are hitting all-time highs. There's risk in all of these stocks, but I'd rather own the stocks where the risks are easier to see and understand. That means Exxon and Chevron would be my pick. Here's why. The capital spending going into artificial intelligence is massive. AI is just a computer program, so it needs electricity to operate. That should lead to strong demand for power. That's the basic story behind companies like Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy. Of the four, Oklo and NuScale are the most speculative. These two companies are attempting to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors. The opportunity could be huge, but at this point both companies are losing money and haven't yet proven their technologies are financially viable. Only the most aggressive investors should be considering them. Bloom Energy and Constellation Energy have established and profitable businesses. Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells that provide off-grid power to AI data centers. Constellation Energy is an independent power producer selling power to the tech companies building out their AI operations. Bloom is the more aggressive option, as investors have priced a lot of good news into the stock. Even after a material pullback, the price-to-earnings ratio is still over 100x. Constellation Energy is probably the best positioned to weather an AI pullback, given the long-term contracts it signs, but irrational investors tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater when things turn south. If the AI bubble bursts, all of these stocks are likely to be hard hit, and the pullback over the last week is a sign of the all-or-nothing approach investors often take with new technologies. Meanwhile, the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has pushed oil prices higher, resulting in strong rallies for Exxon and Chevron. Both energy giants are trading near all-time highs, which is something history has shown won't last. Eventually, oil prices will fall, and so will Exxon and Chevron's stock prices. But I'd still rather own an integrated energy giant over the AI power stocks above. The big reason: the energy cycle is well understood by the market and by these integrated energy giants. They will survive in relative stride if history is any guide. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Exxon and Chevron are standouts in the integrated energy sector because of their long histories of annual dividend increases. Exxon's streak is up to 43 years, while Chevron's streak is at 38 years. Meanwhile, they both have extremely low debt-to-equity ratios, at 0.16x and 0.2x, respectively. When the oil market corrects, they will handle the hit to their businesses in relative stride and, likely, continue to reward shareholders with reliable dividends. It isn't clear what to expect from AI power companies, given that their stocks are being driven higher and lower by rapidly shifting investor sentiment. Some, like Oklo and NuScale, may never achieve profitability. Others, like Bloom Energy and Constellation, may not live up to investor expectations. Chevron and Exxon, on the other hand, have proven they can survive the full energy cycle and, given their strong financial positions, appear well positioned to do so again. I understand why investors are excited about Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy. But I have a hard time quantifying the risk given the AI theme that is moving their stocks higher and lower. If I'm going to take on a risk, I prefer it to be one I can get my head around. The risks Exxon and Chevron face in the oil industry are fairly well defined by history. And so is their ability to deal with those risks. I'd rather own them and collect their reliable above-market yields of 2.2% and 3%, respectively. I don't know what to expect from companies that have tied their futures to a new technology whose future is still uncertain. Chairman and chief executive Mike Wirth, vice chairman Mark Nelson and chief financial officer Eimear Bonner are named as the presenters. The report arrives at a notable moment in the company story. Chevron issued a short advisory announcing the date and format of its latest-quarter earnings conference call and webcast. It is a listen-only session, with dial-in details and a webcast link published on the company website, and a recording is promised afterward. The chief financial officer normally addresses cash flow, the balance sheet and capital allocation, while the chief executive frames strategy and the vice chairman is often asked about upstream and downstream operations. Chevron has also lodged the usual regulatory filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission around earlier quarterly reports, and the latest-quarter release is expected to follow the same pattern, with a press release summarizing results and a detailed filing to follow. The acquisition of Hess was among the largest oil transactions of recent years. For quarterly reporting, the deal changes the base. Production volumes, cost lines and capital spending all now include Hess assets, and comparisons with earlier periods require attention to what was added. Management has talked about cost savings from combining overlapping operations in the Bakken and the Gulf of Mexico, along with the benefits of adding a cash-generative offshore asset that complements the company's own portfolio. Chevron already had a broad international footprint, but Guyana adds a different kind of exposure: offshore production from floating vessels, operated by Exxon Mobil, with a rapid build-out of capacity. The arrangement also means Chevron is a non-operating partner in that venture. It receives its share of output and shares in capital decisions, but the day-to-day development schedule is led by another company. That structure influences how Chevron talks about the asset, putting more emphasis on joint governance, approvals for new phases and shared infrastructure than on drilling details. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. The Permian Basin remains the largest contributor to U.S. production growth for Chevron, supported by acreage in both Texas and New Mexico, extensive water and gas gathering systems and a large mineral position. The company has been moving toward a more mature, steady-state development program in which spending is kept at a level meant to sustain output while generating surplus cash. Metrics that tend to feature include the pace of well completions, average lateral length, productivity per well and operating cost per barrel. Management has also been working on digital tools and simplified well designs to trim costs. Chevron's downstream business is smaller than the upstream arm but still contributes meaningful cash. The company also operates a branded retail network under the Chevron and Texaco names in several parts of the world. West Coast refining has a particular set of challenges. California has tightened regulations and has seen refinery closures, which has made supply tight and prices volatile. Chevron's international portfolio provides diversification and cash flow that does not depend on U.S. shale. The Tengizchevroil venture in Kazakhstan is among the largest oil fields operated by the company, and a major expansion known as the expansion project known as the growth and wellhead pressure management effort has been ramping up. Production there is exported largely through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, so pipeline disruptions or maintenance can affect volumes. In Australia, the Gorgon and Wheatstone liquefied natural gas projects supply customers in Asia under long-term contracts.
